claim: Cavin-3 is a tumor suppressor protein of unknown function.
source: Cavin-3 is a tumor suppressor protein of unknown function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a direct assertion about cavin-3's classification and current understanding.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 increases Akt signaling at the expense of ERK.
source: Loss of cavin-3 increases Akt signaling at the expense of ERK, while gain of cavin-3 increases ERK signaling at the expense Akt.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures including Figure 2B,C and Figure 4B,C showing protein levels of pAkt and pERK.

claim: Gain of cavin-3 increases ERK signaling at the expense of Akt.
source: Loss of cavin-3 increases Akt signaling at the expense of ERK, while gain of cavin-3 increases ERK signaling at the expense Akt.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing that re-expression of cavin-3 in H1299 cells increases pERK and decreases pAkt.

claim: Cavin-3 facilitates signal transduction to ERK by anchoring caveolae to the membrane skeleton of the plasma membrane via myosin-1c.
source: Cavin-3 facilitates signal transduction to ERK by anchoring caveolae to the membrane skeleton of the plasma membrane via myosin-1c.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 5 and 6 showing co-immunoprecipitation of cavin-3 with myosin-1c, and that knockdown of myosin-1c phenocopies cavin-3 knockdown effects.

claim: Caveolae are lipid raft specializations that contain an ERK activation module.
source: Caveolae are lipid raft specializations that contain an ERK activation module and loss of the cavin-3 linkage reduces the abundance of caveolae, thereby separating this ERK activation module from signaling receptors.
evidence: This is supported by fractionation data in Figure 5G showing that MEK and ERK co-fractionate with caveolin-1 in low-density membrane fractions.

claim: Loss of the cavin-3 linkage reduces the abundance of caveolae.
source: Caveolae are lipid raft specializations that contain an ERK activation module and loss of the cavin-3 linkage reduces the abundance of caveolae, thereby separating this ERK activation module from signaling receptors.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 5C showing 87% reduction in caveolae abundance following cavin-3 knockdown.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 promotes Akt signaling through suppression of EGR1 and PTEN.
source: Loss of cavin-3 promotes Akt signaling through suppression of EGR1 and PTEN.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2B, 4B, and 8 showing that loss of cavin-3 reduces EGR1 and PTEN levels, and that ectopic expression of EGR1 suppresses pAkt.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 induces Warburg metabolism (aerobic glycolysis).
source: The in vitro consequences of the loss of cavin-3 include induction of Warburg metabolism (aerobic glycolysis), accelerated cell proliferation, and resistance to apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3C and Figure 4F showing increased glucose consumption and lactate production in cavin-3 depleted cells.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 causes accelerated cell proliferation.
source: The in vitro consequences of the loss of cavin-3 include induction of Warburg metabolism (aerobic glycolysis), accelerated cell proliferation, and resistance to apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2A showing that after 10 days of cavin-3 knockdown, cell proliferation exceeds normal rate.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 causes resistance to apoptosis.
source: The in vitro consequences of the loss of cavin-3 include induction of Warburg metabolism (aerobic glycolysis), accelerated cell proliferation, and resistance to apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2E showing reduced TUNEL staining and PARP1 cleavage in response to TNFα in cavin-3 depleted cells.

claim: The in vivo consequences of cavin-3 knockout are increased lactate production and cachexia.
source: The in vivo consequences of cavin-3 knockout are increased lactate production and cachexia.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 9C showing increased lactate production in lung tissue from Cavin-3 KO mice, and Figure 9E,F showing 40% reduction in body weight and lipodystrophy.

claim: In humans, cavin-3 is encoded in the 11p15.5 tumor suppressor locus.
source: In humans, cavin-3 is encoded in the 11p15.5 tumor suppressor locus and loss of cavin-3 expression is common in many epithelial and glial derived cancers (Zochbauer-Muller et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2008; Martinez et al., 2009; Tong et al., 2010; Caren et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic location of cavin-3 supported by citations.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 expression is common in many epithelial and glial derived cancers.
source: In humans, cavin-3 is encoded in the 11p15.5 tumor suppressor locus and loss of cavin-3 expression is common in many epithelial and glial derived cancers (Zochbauer-Muller et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2008; Martinez et al., 2009; Tong et al., 2010; Caren et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Cavin-3 expression is absent in many cancer cell lines.
source: Cavin-3 expression is also absent in many cancer cell lines and ectopic expression of cavin-3 in these cells is sufficient to suppress their tumorigenesis in athymic mice (Xu et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ectopic expression of cavin-3 in cancer cell lines is sufficient to suppress their tumorigenesis in athymic mice.
source: Cavin-3 expression is also absent in many cancer cell lines and ectopic expression of cavin-3 in these cells is sufficient to suppress their tumorigenesis in athymic mice (Xu et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Forced over-expression of cavin-3 can induce G1 arrest and promote apoptosis.
source: How cavin-3 expression suppresses tumorigenesis is not clear; however, forced over-expression of cavin-3 can induce G1 arrest and promote apoptosis (Lee et al., 2011), suggesting that cavin-3 may suppress mitogenic signaling.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Cavin-3 may suppress mitogenic signaling.
source: How cavin-3 expression suppresses tumorigenesis is not clear; however, forced over-expression of cavin-3 can induce G1 arrest and promote apoptosis (Lee et al., 2011), suggesting that cavin-3 may suppress mitogenic signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from cited data.

claim: Cavin-3 is one of four cavin family members.
source: Cavin-3 is one of four cavin family members, all of which are localized to caveolae (Bastiani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about protein family classification supported by citation.

claim: All cavin family members are localized to caveolae.
source: Cavin-3 is one of four cavin family members, all of which are localized to caveolae (Bastiani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A population of EGF, PDGF, and insulin receptors have been visualized by immuno-EM either in or adjacent to caveolae.
source: Caveolae are invaginated, lipid-raft microdomains of the plasma membrane that may play roles in mitogenic signaling because a population of EGF, PDGF, and insulin receptors have been visualized by immuno-EM either in or adjacent to caveolae (Liu et al., 1996; Foti et al., 2007; Nagy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Caveolae are not required for cell proliferation.
source: Caveolae are not, however, required for cell proliferation because caveolae are not present in all cell types, caveolae do not appear until late in embryogenesis and animals with mutations that prevent caveolae formation are viable and of normal size (Engelman et al., 1998; Drab et al., 2001; Razani et al., 2001, 2002; Fang et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Caveolae are not present in all cell types.
source: Caveolae are not, however, required for cell proliferation because caveolae are not present in all cell types, caveolae do not appear until late in embryogenesis and animals with mutations that prevent caveolae formation are viable and of normal size (Engelman et al., 1998; Drab et al., 2001; Razani et al., 2001, 2002; Fang et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Caveolae do not appear until late in embryogenesis.
source: Caveolae are not, however, required for cell proliferation because caveolae are not present in all cell types, caveolae do not appear until late in embryogenesis and animals with mutations that prevent caveolae formation are viable and of normal size (Engelman et al., 1998; Drab et al., 2001; Razani et al., 2001, 2002; Fang et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Animals with mutations that prevent caveolae formation are viable and of normal size.
source: Caveolae are not, however, required for cell proliferation because caveolae are not present in all cell types, caveolae do not appear until late in embryogenesis and animals with mutations that prevent caveolae formation are viable and of normal size (Engelman et al., 1998; Drab et al., 2001; Razani et al., 2001, 2002; Fang et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some mutations that prevent caveolae formation are associated with hyperplasia and fibrosis in lung.
source: Caveolae may instead limit cell proliferation because some mutations that prevent caveolae formation are associated with hyperplasia and fibrosis in lung (Drab et al., 2001; Razani et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cavin-1 provides a structural function by binding to caveolin-1, stabilizing the invaginated morphology of caveolae and providing an interaction surface for other cavins.
source: Cavin-1 provides a structural function by binding to the principal caveolin, caveolin-1, stabilizing the invaginated morphology of caveolae and providing an interaction surface for other cavins (Hill et al., 2008; Liu and Pilch, 2008; Bastiani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cavin-2 and Cavin-4 show restricted expression and may serve cell-type specific functions.
source: Cavin-2 and Cavin-4 show restricted expression and may serve cell-type specific functions (Bastiani et al., 2009; Hansen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cavin-3 is broadly expressed.
source: By contrast, cavin-3 is broadly expressed and has been proposed to function in caveolae internalization (McMahon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cavin-3 has been proposed to function in caveolae internalization.
source: By contrast, cavin-3 is broadly expressed and has been proposed to function in caveolae internalization (McMahon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Knockdown of cavin-3 suppressed the ability of EGF to induce most immediate early (IE) response genes.
source: Contrary to expectation, microarrays showed that knockdown of cavin-3 suppressed the ability of EGF to induce most immediate early (IE) response genes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Many IE transcripts suppressed by cavin-3 knockdown encoded proteins whose expression is driven by ERK.
source: Suppressed transcripts fell into two categories: those that were fully suppressed by 3 days of knockdown and those that fell gradually during the 15-day time course. Many IE transcripts in the first group encoded proteins whose expression is driven by ERK (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data in Figure 1A,B and published literature on ERK-regulated genes.

claim: 3 days of cavin-3 knockdown is sufficient to inhibit EGF-dependent phosphorylation of ERK.
source: This observation suggested that loss of cavin-3 suppressed ERK signaling and 3 days of knockdown proved sufficient to inhibit EGF-dependent phosphorylation of ERK (pERK), translocation of ERK to the nucleus and induction of the ERK-responsive transcription factor, cFos (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and immunofluorescence data in Figure 1C,D.

claim: 3 days of cavin-3 knockdown inhibits translocation of ERK to the nucleus.
source: This observation suggested that loss of cavin-3 suppressed ERK signaling and 3 days of knockdown proved sufficient to inhibit EGF-dependent phosphorylation of ERK (pERK), translocation of ERK to the nucleus and induction of the ERK-responsive transcription factor, cFos (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1C.

claim: 3 days of cavin-3 knockdown inhibits induction of the ERK-responsive transcription factor, cFos.
source: This observation suggested that loss of cavin-3 suppressed ERK signaling and 3 days of knockdown proved sufficient to inhibit EGF-dependent phosphorylation of ERK (pERK), translocation of ERK to the nucleus and induction of the ERK-responsive transcription factor, cFos (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1D.

claim: 3-day cavin-3 knockdown impairs ERK activation by serum and diverse stimuli.
source: The impact of cavin-3 depletion on ERK signaling was not specific to EGF because 3-day knockdown also impaired ERK activation by serum and diverse stimuli (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1E showing reduced pERK in response to multiple mitogens.

claim: Cavin-3 expression is necessary for efficient ERK activation.
source: Cavin-3 expression is thus necessary for efficient ERK activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing impaired ERK activation upon cavin-3 depletion.

claim: Knockdown of cavin-3 initially slowed cell growth.
source: pERK is a potent driver of cell proliferation and knockdown of cavin-3 initially slowed cell growth; however, proliferation returned to a normal rate after 3 days and exceeded the normal rate after 10 days of knockdown (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data in Figure 2A.

claim: After 3 days of cavin-3 knockdown, cell proliferation returned to a normal rate.
source: pERK is a potent driver of cell proliferation and knockdown of cavin-3 initially slowed cell growth; however, proliferation returned to a normal rate after 3 days and exceeded the normal rate after 10 days of knockdown (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data in Figure 2A.

claim: After 10 days of cavin-3 knockdown, cell proliferation exceeded the normal rate.
source: pERK is a potent driver of cell proliferation and knockdown of cavin-3 initially slowed cell growth; however, proliferation returned to a normal rate after 3 days and exceeded the normal rate after 10 days of knockdown (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data in Figure 2A.

claim: pERK levels did not recover during the 15-day cavin-3 knockdown time course.
source: pERK levels did not recover during the time course (Figure 2B), indicating that cavin-3 depleted cells compensated through other means.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2B.

claim: The transcript whose expression showed the greatest suppression following cavin-3 depletion was early growth response protein 1 (EGR1).
source: To identify the mechanism, we queried the IE microarray data and noted that the transcript whose expression showed the greatest suppression following cavin-3 depletion was early growth response protein 1 (EGR1) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data in Figure 1B.

claim: EGR1 is an ERK-induced transcription factor that drives expression of PTEN.
source: EGR1 is an ERK-induced transcription factor that drives expression of phosphatase and tensin homolog protein (PTEN) (Yu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: PTEN opposes the action of PI3K by dephosphorylating PIP3 back to PIP2.
source: PTEN opposes the action of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) by dephosphorylating phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3) back to phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PTEN function.

claim: PIP3 generation by PI3K is necessary for the recruitment and activation of Akt.
source: PIP3 generation by PI3K is necessary for the recruitment and activation of Akt (Engelman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Knockdown of cavin-3 caused progressive loss of both EGR1 and PTEN.
source: Knockdown of cavin-3 caused progressive loss of both EGR1 and PTEN.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2B.

claim: Loss of EGR1 and PTEN coincided with a fivefold increase in steady state levels of activated Akt (pAkt).
source: Loss of EGR1 and PTEN coincided with a fivefold increase in steady state levels of activated Akt (pAkt) (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and densitometry data in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The switch from ERK to Akt signaling resulted in cell growth that was resistant to the MEK inhibitor, PD98059.
source: The switch from ERK to Akt signaling resulted in cell growth that was resistant to the MAPK/ERK Kinase (MEK) inhibitor, PD98059, and more sensitive to the PI3K inhibitor, LY294002 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data in Figure 2D.

claim: The switch from ERK to Akt signaling resulted in cell growth that was more sensitive to the PI3K inhibitor, LY294002.
source: The switch from ERK to Akt signaling resulted in cell growth that was resistant to the MAPK/ERK Kinase (MEK) inhibitor, PD98059, and more sensitive to the PI3K inhibitor, LY294002 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data in Figure 2D.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 shifts cellular signaling to an Akt-dominated state.
source: These findings show that loss of cavin-3 shifts cellular signaling to an Akt-dominated state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased pAkt and decreased pERK.

claim: Activation of Akt can suppress apoptosis through inhibition of cytochrome c release from mitochondria and induction of inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (IAPs).
source: Activation of Akt can suppress apoptosis through inhibition of cytochrome c release from mitochondria and induction of inhibitor of apoptosis proteins (IAPs) (Kennedy et al., 1999; Papapetropoulos et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Treatment of SV589 fibroblasts with TNFα potently induced apoptosis.
source: Treatment of SV589 fibroblasts with TNFα potently induced apoptosis as evidenced by the robust cleavage of the caspase-3 target, Poly [ADP-Ribose] Polymerase 1 (PARP1), and the prevalence of TUNEL positive cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL and PARP1 cleavage data in Figure 2E.

claim: Knockdown of cavin-3 progressively reduced cell sensitivity to TNFα.
source: Knockdown of cavin-3 progressively reduced cell sensitivity to TNFα in both assays.
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL and PARP1 cleavage data in Figure 2E.

claim: Resistance to TNFα correlated with induction of the IAP, survivin.
source: Resistance to TNFα correlated with induction of the IAP, survivin (Figure 2B), one of several anti-apoptosis proteins induced by Akt (Duronio, 2008; Guha and Altieri, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2B and citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 inhibits apoptosis.
source: These findings show that loss of cavin-3 inhibits apoptosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TNFα resistance data.

claim: Akt can promote cell proliferation through activation of mTORC1.
source: Akt can also promote cell proliferation through activation of the mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) (Manning and Cantley, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: mTORC1 activates many biosynthetic pathways through phosphorylation and activation of S6K.
source: mTORC1 activates many biosynthetic pathways through phosphorylation and activation of S6K (Duvel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 potently increased levels of phosphorylated S6K (pS6K).
source: Loss of cavin-3 potently increased levels of phosphorylated S6K (pS6K) (Figure 2B), indicating that cavin-3 loss activates mTORC1.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2B.

claim: Cavin-3 loss activates mTORC1.
source: Loss of cavin-3 potently increased levels of phosphorylated S6K (pS6K) (Figure 2B), indicating that cavin-3 loss activates mTORC1.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in pS6K, a known mTORC1 target.

claim: The rapid proliferation of 15-day knockdown cells was associated with substantial changes in gene transcription.
source: Microarrays comparing transcript profiles cells depleted of cavin-3 for 0, 3, 8, and 15 days showed that the rapid proliferation of 15-day knockdown cells was associated with substantial changes in gene transcription (Figures 1A and 3A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data in Figures 1A and 3A.

claim: Many transcripts that were up-regulated in the 15-day knockdowns are part of protein and nucleic acid biosynthetic pathways.
source: Many of transcripts that were up-regulated in the 15-day knockdowns are part of protein and nucleic acid biosynthetic pathways (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis of microarray data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Entry into aerobic glycolysis normally requires hypoxia induced factor 1 (HIF1).
source: Entry into aerobic glycolysis normally requires hypoxia induced factor 1 (HIF1), a transcription factor whose activity is controlled by the protein level of its α-subunit (HIF1α) (Lunt and Vander Heiden, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Akt and mTORC1 increase HIF1α protein levels.
source: Akt and mTORC1 increase HIF1α protein levels (Schleicher et al., 2009; Duvel et al., 2010) and knockdown of cavin-3 progressively increased both HIF1α levels and the use of fermentative glycolysis (Figures 2B and 3C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Knockdown of cavin-3 progressively increased both HIF1α levels and the use of fermentative glycolysis.
source: Akt and mTORC1 increase HIF1α protein levels (Schleicher et al., 2009; Duvel et al., 2010) and knockdown of cavin-3 progressively increased both HIF1α levels and the use of fermentative glycolysis (Figures 2B and 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2B and glucose/lactate assay data in Figure 3C.

claim: Glucose consumption and lactate production in 15-day cavin-3 knockdown cells reached rates equivalent to those observed in H1299 cells.
source: Glucose consumption and lactate production reached rates that were equivalent to those observed in H1299 cells, a non-small cell lung carcinoma cell line that lacks cavin-3 expression (Xu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by glucose/lactate assay data in Figure 3C and citation.

claim: H1299 is a non-small cell lung carcinoma cell line that lacks cavin-3 expression.
source: Glucose consumption and lactate production reached rates that were equivalent to those observed in H1299 cells, a non-small cell lung carcinoma cell line that lacks cavin-3 expression (Xu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Prolonged loss of cavin-3 activates the Akt/mTORC1/HIF1 pathway and induces aerobic glycolysis.
source: These findings show that prolonged loss of cavin-3 activates the Akt/mTORC1/HIF1 pathway and induces aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased pAkt, pS6K, HIF1α, and glycolysis.

claim: Activation of Akt/mTORC1/HIF1 pathway likely facilitates rapid cell proliferation.
source: Activation of these pathways likely facilitates rapid cell proliferation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed correlation between pathway activation and increased proliferation.

claim: Embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from cavin-3 knockout animals displayed reduced levels of pERK, EGR1 and PTEN.
source: As observed with 15-day knockdowns in SV589 cells, embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from cavin-3 knockout (Cavin-3 KO, Prkcdbp−/−) animals displayed reduced levels of pERK, EGR1 and PTEN, elevated levels of survivin, pAkt, pS6K and HIF1α, increased rates of fermentative glycolysis, faster proliferation, heightened sensitivity to LY294002, resistance to PD98059 and insensitivity to TNFα as compared to wild-type MEFs (Figure 4B–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4B.

claim: Embryonic fibroblasts from cavin-3 knockout animals displayed elevated levels of survivin, pAkt, pS6K and HIF1α.
source: As observed with 15-day knockdowns in SV589 cells, embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from cavin-3 knockout (Cavin-3 KO, Prkcdbp−/−) animals displayed reduced levels of pERK, EGR1 and PTEN, elevated levels of survivin, pAkt, pS6K and HIF1α, increased rates of fermentative glycolysis, faster proliferation, heightened sensitivity to LY294002, resistance to PD98059 and insensitivity to TNFα as compared to wild-type MEFs (Figure 4B–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4B.

claim: Cavin-3 KO MEFs showed increased rates of fermentative glycolysis compared to wild-type MEFs.
source: As observed with 15-day knockdowns in SV589 cells, embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from cavin-3 knockout (Cavin-3 KO, Prkcdbp−/−) animals displayed reduced levels of pERK, EGR1 and PTEN, elevated levels of survivin, pAkt, pS6K and HIF1α, increased rates of fermentative glycolysis, faster proliferation, heightened sensitivity to LY294002, resistance to PD98059 and insensitivity to TNFα as compared to wild-type MEFs (Figure 4B–G).
evidence: This is supported by glucose/lactate assay data in Figure 4F.

claim: Cavin-3 KO MEFs showed faster proliferation compared to wild-type MEFs.
source: As observed with 15-day knockdowns in SV589 cells, embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from cavin-3 knockout (Cavin-3 KO, Prkcdbp−/−) animals displayed reduced levels of pERK, EGR1 and PTEN, elevated levels of survivin, pAkt, pS6K and HIF1α, increased rates of fermentative glycolysis, faster proliferation, heightened sensitivity to LY294002, resistance to PD98059 and insensitivity to TNFα as compared to wild-type MEFs (Figure 4B–G).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data in Figure 4E.

claim: Cavin-3 KO MEFs showed heightened sensitivity to LY294002 compared to wild-type MEFs.
source: As observed with 15-day knockdowns in SV589 cells, embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from cavin-3 knockout (Cavin-3 KO, Prkcdbp−/−) animals displayed reduced levels of pERK, EGR1 and PTEN, elevated levels of survivin, pAkt, pS6K and HIF1α, increased rates of fermentative glycolysis, faster proliferation, heightened sensitivity to LY294002, resistance to PD98059 and insensitivity to TNFα as compared to wild-type MEFs (Figure 4B–G).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data in Figure 4D.

claim: Cavin-3 KO MEFs showed resistance to PD98059 compared to wild-type MEFs.
source: As observed with 15-day knockdowns in SV589 cells, embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from cavin-3 knockout (Cavin-3 KO, Prkcdbp−/−) animals displayed reduced levels of pERK, EGR1 and PTEN, elevated levels of survivin, pAkt, pS6K and HIF1α, increased rates of fermentative glycolysis, faster proliferation, heightened sensitivity to LY294002, resistance to PD98059 and insensitivity to TNFα as compared to wild-type MEFs (Figure 4B–G).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data in Figure 4D.

claim: Cavin-3 KO MEFs showed insensitivity to TNFα compared to wild-type MEFs.
source: As observed with 15-day knockdowns in SV589 cells, embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from cavin-3 knockout (Cavin-3 KO, Prkcdbp−/−) animals displayed reduced levels of pERK, EGR1 and PTEN, elevated levels of survivin, pAkt, pS6K and HIF1α, increased rates of fermentative glycolysis, faster proliferation, heightened sensitivity to LY294002, resistance to PD98059 and insensitivity to TNFα as compared to wild-type MEFs (Figure 4B–G).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL and PARP1 cleavage data in Figure 4G.

claim: Genetic ablation of cavin-3 expression recapitulates phenotypes induced following long-term knockdown of cavin-3 by siRNA.
source: Thus, genetic ablation of cavin-3 expression recapitulates phenotypes induced following long-term knockdown of cavin-3 by siRNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the phenotypes of Cavin-3 KO MEFs with 15-day knockdown cells.

claim: Knockdown of cavin-3 did not inhibit EGF-dependent autophosphorylation of EGF receptors.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, knockdown of cavin-3 did not inhibit EGF-dependent autophosphorylation of EGF receptors (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5A showing pEGFR levels.

claim: Inhibition of protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) was unable to activate ERK despite potent activation of Akt in cells depleted for cavin-3.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A), which normally prevents the basal activity of mitogen receptors from activating downstream signaling cascades (Wang et al., 2003; Van Kanegan et al., 2005), was unable to activate ERK despite potent activation of Akt in cells depleted for cavin-3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5B showing pERK and pAkt levels after calyculin-A treatment.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 disrupts signal transduction coupling between mitogen receptors and ERK.
source: These findings indicate that loss of cavin-3 disrupts signal transduction coupling between mitogen receptors and ERK.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that receptor autophosphorylation is intact but ERK activation is impaired.

claim: Knockdown of cavin-3 redistributes caveolin-1 to the cell interior by immunofluorescence.
source: We found that knockdown of cavin-3 both reduced caveolae abundance and re-localized the principal caveolae coat protein, caveolin-1, to the Golgi region (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C.

claim: The reduction in caveolae abundance correlated with loss of ERK responsiveness to EGF.
source: The reduction in caveolae abundance correlated with loss of ERK responsiveness to EGF (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5D.

claim: Cavin-3 is necessary for surface caveolae.
source: These findings indicate that cavin-3 is necessary for surface caveolae and suggest that caveolae facilitate signal transduction to ERK.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that cavin-3 knockdown reduces caveolae abundance.

claim: Caveolae facilitate signal transduction to ERK.
source: These findings indicate that cavin-3 is necessary for surface caveolae and suggest that caveolae facilitate signal transduction to ERK.
evidence: This is suggested based on the correlation between caveolae loss and ERK signaling impairment.

claim: Caveolae associate with actin filaments at the plasma membrane.
source: Caveolae associate with actin filaments at the plasma membrane (Rohlich and Allison, 1976; Singer, 1979) and disruption of F-actin impaired mitogen-dependent stimulation of ERK to the same extent as cavin-3 depletion (Figure 5D; Aplin and Juliano, 1999), suggesting that cavin-3 may increase caveolae abundance by anchoring caveolae to F-actin at the cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Disruption of F-actin impaired mitogen-dependent stimulation of ERK to the same extent as cavin-3 depletion.
source: Caveolae associate with actin filaments at the plasma membrane (Rohlich and Allison, 1976; Singer, 1979) and disruption of F-actin impaired mitogen-dependent stimulation of ERK to the same extent as cavin-3 depletion (Figure 5D; Aplin and Juliano, 1999), suggesting that cavin-3 may increase caveolae abundance by anchoring caveolae to F-actin at the cell surface.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5D showing pERK levels after latrunculin-A treatment.

claim: Cavin-3 may increase caveolae abundance by anchoring caveolae to F-actin at the cell surface.
source: Caveolae associate with actin filaments at the plasma membrane (Rohlich and Allison, 1976; Singer, 1979) and disruption of F-actin impaired mitogen-dependent stimulation of ERK to the same extent as cavin-3 depletion (Figure 5D; Aplin and Juliano, 1999), suggesting that cavin-3 may increase caveolae abundance by anchoring caveolae to F-actin at the cell surface.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the similar effects of cavin-3 depletion and F-actin disruption.

claim: Myosin-1c co-localizes with caveolin-1.
source: Myosin-1c satisfied all five criteria (Figure 5C–F), indicating that myosin-1c participates in a cavin-3 linkage that anchors caveolae to peripheral actin.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5E.

claim: Myosin-1c associates with cavin-3.
source: Myosin-1c satisfied all five criteria (Figure 5C–F), indicating that myosin-1c participates in a cavin-3 linkage that anchors caveolae to peripheral actin.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5F.

claim: Knockdown of myosin-1c mislocalizes caveolin-1.
source: Myosin-1c satisfied all five criteria (Figure 5C–F), indicating that myosin-1c participates in a cavin-3 linkage that anchors caveolae to peripheral actin.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C.

claim: Knockdown of myosin-1c impairs ERK activation.
source: Myosin-1c satisfied all five criteria (Figure 5C–F), indicating that myosin-1c participates in a cavin-3 linkage that anchors caveolae to peripheral actin.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 5D.

claim: Myosin-1c participates in a cavin-3 linkage that anchors caveolae to peripheral actin.
source: Myosin-1c satisfied all five criteria (Figure 5C–F), indicating that myosin-1c participates in a cavin-3 linkage that anchors caveolae to peripheral actin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the five criteria satisfied by myosin-1c.

claim: MEK and ERK have been shown to co-fractionate with mitogen receptors and caveolin-1 in cellular membranes of low protein-to-lipid density.
source: MEK and ERK have been shown to co-fractionate with mitogen receptors and caveolin-1 in cellular membranes of low protein-to-lipid density (Liu et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: EGFR, caveolin-1, MEK and ERK co-fractionated in low-density membrane fractions isolated from untreated SV589 fibroblasts.
source: Consistent with these published observations, we found that EGFR, caveolin-1, MEK and ERK co-fractionated in low-density membrane fractions isolated from untreated SV589 fibroblasts; however, knockdown of cavin-3, knockdown of myosin-1c or brief treatment with the actin-depolymerization compound, latrunculin-A, caused MEK and ERK to accumulate in the high-density fractions, which contain the bulk of cellular membrane protein (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by fractionation and immunoblot data in Figure 5G.

claim: Knockdown of cavin-3, knockdown of myosin-1c or brief treatment with latrunculin-A caused MEK and ERK to accumulate in high-density membrane fractions.
source: Consistent with these published observations, we found that EGFR, caveolin-1, MEK and ERK co-fractionated in low-density membrane fractions isolated from untreated SV589 fibroblasts; however, knockdown of cavin-3, knockdown of myosin-1c or brief treatment with the actin-depolymerization compound, latrunculin-A, caused MEK and ERK to accumulate in the high-density fractions, which contain the bulk of cellular membrane protein (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by fractionation and immunoblot data in Figure 5G.

claim: A cytoskeletal linkage involving cavin-3, myosin-1c and F-actin positions MEK and ERK for activation by mitogen receptors.
source: These observations indicate that a cytoskeletal linkage involving cavin-3, myosin-1c and F-actin positions MEK and ERK for activation by mitogen receptors, most likely by anchoring caveolae at the cell surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fractionation data showing that disruption of the linkage separates MEK/ERK from receptors.

claim: In addition to cavin-3, both cavin-1 and caveolin-1 co-precipitated with myosin-1c.
source: We tested whether cavin-1 and caveolin-1 are components of the cavin-3 linkage using immunoprecipitation with antibodies to myosin-1c and found that in addition to cavin-3 both cavin-1 and caveolin-1 co-precipitated with myosin-1c (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6A.

claim: Knockdowns of caveolin-1 and cavin-1 increased pAkt at the expense of pERK.
source: Like the cavin-3 and myosin-1c knockdowns, knockdowns of caveolin-1 and cavin-1 increased pAkt at the expense of pERK (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and densitometry data in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Knockdown of cavin-1 reduced the protein level of cavin-3.
source: However, unlike the myosin-1c knockdown, knockdown of cavin-1 reduced the protein level of cavin-3, while knockdown of caveolin-1 reduced protein levels of both cavin-1 and cavin-3.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6B.

claim: Knockdown of caveolin-1 reduced protein levels of both cavin-1 and cavin-3.
source: However, unlike the myosin-1c knockdown, knockdown of cavin-1 reduced the protein level of cavin-3, while knockdown of caveolin-1 reduced protein levels of both cavin-1 and cavin-3.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6B.

claim: Cavin-3 over-expression partially protected cavin-3 levels from knockdown of cavin-1, cavin-3 or caveolin-1.
source: Cavin-3 over-expression partially protected cavin-3 levels from knockdown of cavin-1, cavin-3 or caveolin-1.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6E.

claim: Protection of cavin-3 levels muted the effects of cavin-1, cavin-3, and caveolin-1 knockdowns on pERK and pAkt levels.
source: This protection muted the effects of these knockdowns on pERK and pAkt levels (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and densitometry data in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Cavin-3 levels correlated better with pERK/ERK and pAkt/Akt ratios than did levels of either cavin-1 or caveolin-1.
source: Importantly, cavin-3 levels correlated better with pERK/ERK and pAkt/Akt ratios than did levels of either cavin-1 or caveolin-1 (Figure 6C,F,G).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis in Figure 6G.

claim: Cavin-3 is the limiting component of the cavin/caveolin complex for caveolar influence on ERK and Akt signaling.
source: The strength of this correlation suggests that cavin-3 is the limiting component of the cavin/caveolin complex for caveolar influence on ERK and Akt signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong correlation between cavin-3 levels and signaling outcomes.

claim: Caveolin-1 and cavin-1 are required for normal abundance of caveolae.
source: Both caveolin-1 and cavin-1 are required for normal abundance of caveolae (Drab et al., 2001; Razani et al., 2001; Hill et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Caveolin-1 is an integral membrane protein that polymerizes to form filaments that coat the cytosolic surface of caveolae.
source: Caveolin-1 is an integral membrane protein that polymerizes to form filaments that coat the cytosolic surface of caveolae (Fernandez et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cavin-1 has been proposed to serve as an adaptor that links other cavins to the caveolin coat.
source: Cavin-1 has been proposed to serve as an adaptor that links other cavins to the caveolin coat (Bastiani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cavin-3 promotes efficient signal transduction to ERK by bridging between the cavin-1/caveolin-1 complex and myosin-1c.
source: We propose that cavin-3 promotes efficient signal transduction to ERK by bridging between the cavin-1/caveolin-1 complex and myosin-1c (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing interactions and functional dependencies.

claim: H1299 cells lacked detectable cavin-3, but exhibited levels of cavin-1, caveolin-1, myosin-1c and actin that were similar to the endogenous levels of SV589 fibroblasts.
source: H1299 cells are a line of non-small cell lung carcinoma cells that lacked detectable cavin-3, but exhibited levels of cavin-1, caveolin-1, myosin-1c and actin that were similar to the endogenous levels of SV589 fibroblasts (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7A.

claim: H1299 cells had pERK and pAkt responses that were similar to SV589 fibroblasts following cavin-3 knockdown.
source: Comparison of the pERK and pAkt responses to mitogens showed that H1299 cells had pERK and pAkt responses that were similar to SV589 fibroblasts following cavin-3 knockdown (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Re-expression of cavin-3 restored the cavin-3 linkage in H1299 cells.
source: Re-expression of cavin-3 restored the cavin-3 linkage as evidenced by the ability of myosin-1c antibody to co-precipitate cavin-1, cavin-3, and myosin-1c from lysates of H/Cavin-3 cells, but not H/GFP cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7C.

claim: Restoration of the cavin-3 linkage resulted in a 7.6-fold increase in surface caveolae.
source: Restoration of the cavin-3 linkage resulted in a 7.6-fold increase in surface caveolae and redistribution of caveolin-1 to the plasma membrane (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy quantification in Figure 7D.

claim: Restoration of the cavin-3 linkage resulted in redistribution of caveolin-1 to the plasma membrane.
source: Restoration of the cavin-3 linkage resulted in a 7.6-fold increase in surface caveolae and redistribution of caveolin-1 to the plasma membrane (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7D.

claim: H/Cavin-3 cells displayed higher levels of pERK and EGR1 compared to parental H1299 or H/GFP cells.
source: As compared to parental H1299 or H/GFP cells, H/Cavin-3 cells displayed higher levels of pERK and EGR1 (Figure 7B,E); lower levels of pAkt, HIF1α and pS6K (Figure 7B,E); and increased sensitivity to PD98059 and resistance to LY294002 (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and densitometry data in Figure 7B,E.

claim: H/Cavin-3 cells displayed lower levels of pAkt, HIF1α and pS6K compared to parental H1299 or H/GFP cells.
source: As compared to parental H1299 or H/GFP cells, H/Cavin-3 cells displayed higher levels of pERK and EGR1 (Figure 7B,E); lower levels of pAkt, HIF1α and pS6K (Figure 7B,E); and increased sensitivity to PD98059 and resistance to LY294002 (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and densitometry data in Figure 7B,E.

claim: H/Cavin-3 cells showed increased sensitivity to PD98059 and resistance to LY294002 compared to H/GFP cells.
source: As compared to parental H1299 or H/GFP cells, H/Cavin-3 cells displayed higher levels of pERK and EGR1 (Figure 7B,E); lower levels of pAkt, HIF1α and pS6K (Figure 7B,E); and increased sensitivity to PD98059 and resistance to LY294002 (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data in Figure 7F.

claim: Signaling changes in H/Cavin-3 cells correlated with reductions in the rate of cell growth, glucose uptake and lactate production.
source: These signaling changes correlated with reductions in the rate of cell growth, glucose uptake and lactate production (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting and glucose/lactate assay data in Figure 7G,H.

claim: Cavin-3 re-expression suppressed survivin levels and sensitized cells to TNFα-dependent apoptosis.
source: Cavin-3 re-expression also suppressed survivin levels and sensitized cells to TNFα-dependent apoptosis (Figure 7B,I).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and TUNEL data in Figure 7B,I.

claim: Restoration of the cavin-3 linkage in cancer cells can normalize ERK/Akt signaling, cell metabolism and apoptosis sensitivity.
source: These findings show that restoration of the cavin-3 linkage in cancer cells can normalize ERK/Akt signaling, cell metabolism and apoptosis sensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the H1299 rescue experiments.

claim: Expression of EGR1 in Cavin-3 KO MEFs suppressed pAkt levels to the same extent as expression of cavin-3.
source: Expression of EGR1 in either Cavin-3 KO MEFs or H1299 cells suppressed pAkt levels to the same extent as expression of cavin-3 (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and densitometry data in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Expression of EGR1 in H1299 cells suppressed pAkt levels to the same extent as expression of cavin-3.
source: Expression of EGR1 in either Cavin-3 KO MEFs or H1299 cells suppressed pAkt levels to the same extent as expression of cavin-3 (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and densitometry data in Figure 8A,B.

claim: EGR1 acts downstream of cavin-3 to suppress Akt activation.
source: These observations indicate that EGR1 acts downstream of cavin-3 to suppress Akt activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that EGR1 expression can substitute for cavin-3 in suppressing pAkt.

claim: Expression of neither EGR1 nor cavin-3 substantially improved PTEN expression in H1299 cells despite potent suppression of pAkt.
source: Interestingly, while expression of either EGR1 or cavin-3 restored PTEN expression to a normal level in Cavin-3 KO MEFs, expression of neither EGR1 nor cavin-3 substantially improved PTEN expression in H1299 cells despite potent suppression of pAkt.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 8A.

claim: The PTEN promoter in H1299 cells is hypermethylated.
source: The PTEN promoter in H1299 cells is hypermethylated (Soria et al., 2002) and this methylation may limit the ability of EGR1 to drive PTEN expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: EGR1 suppresses Akt activation through mechanisms that are independent of PTEN protein level.
source: The ability of cavin-3 and EGR1 to nonetheless suppress Akt activation indicates that EGR1 suppresses Akt activation through mechanisms that are independent of PTEN protein level.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pAkt is suppressed without PTEN restoration in H1299 cells.

claim: Expression of EGR1 was sufficient to suppress aerobic glycolysis in both Cavin-3 KO MEFs and H1299 cells.
source: Expression of EGR1 was sufficient to suppress aerobic glycolysis in both Cavin-3 KO MEFs and H1299 cells (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by glucose/lactate assay data in Figure 8C.

claim: EGR1 expression suppressed both pS6K and HIF1α levels in Cavin-3 KO MEFs and H1299 cells.
source: EGR1 expression suppressed both pS6K and HIF1α levels in both cell lines (Figure 8A) and loss of HIF1α correlated with reductions in glucose consumption and lactate production (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 8A.

claim: Loss of HIF1α correlated with reductions in glucose consumption and lactate production.
source: EGR1 expression suppressed both pS6K and HIF1α levels in both cell lines (Figure 8A) and loss of HIF1α correlated with reductions in glucose consumption and lactate production (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by glucose/lactate assay data in Figure 8C.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 induces aerobic glycolysis via loss of EGR1-dependent suppression of the Akt/mTORC1/HIF1 pathway.
source: Akt and mTORC1 induce HIF1α and the ability of EGR1 to suppress Akt activation indicates that loss of cavin-3 induces aerobic glycolysis via loss of EGR1-dependent suppression of the Akt/mTORC1/HIF1 pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that EGR1 expression suppresses the pathway and glycolysis.

claim: Only cavin-3 re-expression was able to rescue sensitivity to TNFα.
source: In contrast to the effects of EGR1 on cell metabolism, only cavin-3 re-expression was able to rescue sensitivity to TNFα (Figure 8D), indicating that cavin-3 supports an EGR1-independent process that is necessary for TNFα-sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL and PARP1 cleavage data in Figure 8D.

claim: Cavin-3 supports an EGR1-independent process that is necessary for TNFα-sensitivity.
source: In contrast to the effects of EGR1 on cell metabolism, only cavin-3 re-expression was able to rescue sensitivity to TNFα (Figure 8D), indicating that cavin-3 supports an EGR1-independent process that is necessary for TNFα-sensitivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that EGR1 expression does not rescue TNFα sensitivity.

claim: Expression of EGR1 did not restore pERK levels.
source: Expression of EGR1 also did not restore pERK levels (Figure 8A,B) or drive caveolin-1 to the plasma membrane (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and densitometry data in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Expression of EGR1 did not drive caveolin-1 to the plasma membrane.
source: Expression of EGR1 also did not restore pERK levels (Figure 8A,B) or drive caveolin-1 to the plasma membrane (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 8E.

claim: Active ERK facilitates apoptosis through both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways.
source: Active ERK facilitates apoptosis through both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways (Cagnol and Chambard, 2010) and the ability of cavin-3 to support normal apoptosis sensitivity may require both the EGR1-dependent reduction in pAkt and a caveolae-dependent increase in pERK.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The ability of cavin-3 to support normal apoptosis sensitivity may require both the EGR1-dependent reduction in pAkt and a caveolae-dependent increase in pERK.
source: Active ERK facilitates apoptosis through both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways (Cagnol and Chambard, 2010) and the ability of cavin-3 to support normal apoptosis sensitivity may require both the EGR1-dependent reduction in pAkt and a caveolae-dependent increase in pERK.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that both pathways are affected by cavin-3.

claim: Cavin-3 activates at least two processes: (i) an EGR1-dependent process that suppresses the Akt/mTORC1/HIF1 pathway; and (ii) an EGR1-independent process that is necessary for normal apoptosis.
source: Together, these findings show that cavin-3 activates at least two processes: (i) an EGR1-dependent process that suppresses the Akt/mTORC1/HIF1 pathway; and (ii) an EGR1-independent process that is necessary for normal apoptosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EGR1 rescue experiments showing partial rescue of phenotypes.

claim: Lung tissue from Cavin-3 KO animals showed decreased pERK, EGR1, and PTEN levels compared to lung tissue from wild-type animals.
source: Lung tissue from Prkcdbp−/− (Cavin-3 KO) animals showed decreased pERK, EGR1, and PTEN levels and increased pAkt and HIF1α levels as compared to lung tissue from wild-type animals (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and densitometry data in Figure 9A,B.

claim: Lung tissue from Cavin-3 KO animals showed increased pAkt and HIF1α levels compared to lung tissue from wild-type animals.
source: Lung tissue from Prkcdbp−/− (Cavin-3 KO) animals showed decreased pERK, EGR1, and PTEN levels and increased pAkt and HIF1α levels as compared to lung tissue from wild-type animals (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and densitometry data in Figure 9A,B.

claim: The elevated HIF1α of Cavin-3 KO lung tissue was associated with increased fermentative glycolysis ex vivo.
source: The elevated HIF1α of Cavin-3 KO lung tissue was associated with increased fermentative glycolysis ex vivo (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by glucose/lactate assay data in Figure 9C.

claim: In vivo loss of cavin-3 promoted Akt signaling at the expense of ERK and increased glycolytic metabolism.
source: Thus, in vivo loss of cavin-3 promoted Akt signaling at the expense of ERK and increased glycolytic metabolism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo data in Figure 9A-C.

claim: Cavin-3 KO mice had shorter lifespan than control animals.
source: Cavin-3 KO mice did have shorter lifespan than control animals (Figure 9D) and the principal cause of death was cachexia as exemplified by a 40% reduction in body weight and severe lipodystrophy (Figure 9E,F).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival data in Figure 9D.

claim: The principal cause of death in Cavin-3 KO mice was cachexia as exemplified by a 40% reduction in body weight and severe lipodystrophy.
source: Cavin-3 KO mice did have shorter lifespan than control animals (Figure 9D) and the principal cause of death was cachexia as exemplified by a 40% reduction in body weight and severe lipodystrophy (Figure 9E,F).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data in Figure 9E and fat pad images in Figure 9F.

claim: Lipodystrophy is frequently associated with hepatic steatosis.
source: Lipodystrophy is frequently associated with hepatic steatosis (Huang-Doran et al., 2010) and areas of steatosis were observed in livers of Cavin-3 KO animals (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Areas of steatosis were observed in livers of Cavin-3 KO animals.
source: Lipodystrophy is frequently associated with hepatic steatosis (Huang-Doran et al., 2010) and areas of steatosis were observed in livers of Cavin-3 KO animals (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining in Figure 9G.

claim: No lung cancers were observed in Cavin-3 KO animals.
source: Despite the strong association of lung cancer with loss of cavin-3 expression (Zochbauer-Muller et al., 2005), we did not observe lung cancers and saw no differences in lung structure or alveolar density (Figure 9G,H).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis in Figure 9G,H.

claim: No differences in lung structure or alveolar density were observed between Cavin-3 KO and wild-type animals.
source: Despite the strong association of lung cancer with loss of cavin-3 expression (Zochbauer-Muller et al., 2005), we did not observe lung cancers and saw no differences in lung structure or alveolar density (Figure 9G,H).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining and mean linear intercept analysis in Figure 9G,H.

claim: Genetic ablation of cavin-3 expression increases Akt signaling at the expense of ERK, increases the use of fermentative glycolysis in tissues and causes cachexia, but is not sufficient to cause substantial de novo tumorigenesis.
source: Thus, genetic ablation of cavin-3 expression increases Akt signaling at the expense of ERK, increases the use of fermentative glycolysis in tissues and causes cachexia, but is not sufficient to cause substantial de novo tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo phenotypic analysis of Cavin-3 KO mice.

claim: The cavin-3 dependent coupling of caveolae to F-actin is analogous to linkages that generate other specialized domains of the plasma membrane.
source: The cavin-3 dependent coupling of caveolae to F-actin is analogous to linkages that generate other specialized domains of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a conceptual comparison based on known properties of membrane skeleton linkages.

claim: Peripheral F-actin is crosslinked by spectrins into a viscoelastic network (the membrane skeleton) that associates with the plasma membrane through diverse linkages.
source: Peripheral F-actin is crosslinked by spectrins into a viscoelastic network (the membrane skeleton) that associates with the plasma membrane through diverse linkages.
evidence: This is established knowledge about membrane skeleton structure.

claim: The spatial organization of specific linkages allows the membrane skeleton to generate specializations within the plasma membrane.
source: The spatial organization of specific linkages allows the membrane skeleton to generate specializations within the plasma membrane and loss of different organizing linkages results in loss of specific specialized domains (Bennett and Healy, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of different organizing linkages results in loss of specific specialized domains.
source: The spatial organization of specific linkages allows the membrane skeleton to generate specializations within the plasma membrane and loss of different organizing linkages results in loss of specific specialized domains (Bennett and Healy, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cavin-3 is part of a linkage necessary for the caveolae specialization.
source: Our findings show that cavin-3 is part of a linkage necessary for the caveolae specialization (Figures 5–7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing cavin-3's role in caveolae anchoring.

claim: Insulin receptors associate with F-actin and are enriched at the border between caveolae and the rest of the plasma membrane.
source: Intriguingly, insulin receptors also associate with F-actin and are enriched at the border between caveolae and the rest of the plasma membrane (Foti et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The combination of a receptor-actin linkage with the cavin-3 linkage suggests that the skeleton assembles mitogen receptors with the caveolar ERK activation module to facilitate signal transduction coupling.
source: The combination of a receptor-actin linkage with the cavin-3 linkage suggests that the skeleton assembles mitogen receptors with the caveolar ERK activation module to facilitate signal transduction coupling (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed linkages and their functional consequences.

claim: The sophistication of the skeleton correlates with the degree of cellular differentiation.
source: Skeleton-dependent integration of signaling pathways may promote cell differentiation because the sophistication of the skeleton correlates with the degree of cellular differentiation (Bennett and Healy, 2008) and defects in the skeleton are associated with dedifferentiation, increased cell proliferation and resistance to anoikis (Mishra et al., 2005; Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Defects in the skeleton are associated with dedifferentiation, increased cell proliferation and resistance to anoikis.
source: Skeleton-dependent integration of signaling pathways may promote cell differentiation because the sophistication of the skeleton correlates with the degree of cellular differentiation (Bennett and Healy, 2008) and defects in the skeleton are associated with dedifferentiation, increased cell proliferation and resistance to anoikis (Mishra et al., 2005; Kumar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The use of myosin-1c may couple delivery of caveolar components with caveolae anchorage.
source: First, myosin-1c participates in the transport of lipid raft components (Bond et al., 2013) and the use of myosin-1c may couple delivery of caveolar components with caveolae anchorage.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on known functions of myosin-1c.

claim: Myosin-1c participates in the transport of lipid raft components.
source: First, myosin-1c participates in the transport of lipid raft components (Bond et al., 2013) and the use of myosin-1c may couple delivery of caveolar components with caveolae anchorage.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Myosin-1c may control movement of caveolae vesicles within the cortical actin network.
source: Second, caveolae are endocytic structures and myosin-1c may control movement of caveolae vesicles within the cortical actin network.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the motor function of myosin-1c.

claim: The majority of caveolae-derived vesicles remain at the cell periphery where they re-fuse with the plasma membrane in a cyclic process referred to as potocytosis.
source: The majority of caveolae-derived vesicles remain at the cell periphery where they re-fuse with the plasma membrane in a cyclic process referred to as potocytosis (Anderson et al., 1992; Boucrot et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Calcium channels are enriched in caveolae.
source: Myosin-1c may drive caveolae-derived vesicles back to the cell surface in a calcium-regulated manner because calcium channels are enriched in caveolae (Isshiki et al., 1998; Pani and Singh, 2009), the Donnan effects generated by endocytosis promote calcium channel opening (Saito et al., 2007) and calcium promotes both myosin-1c motor activity (Barylko et al., 1992; Zhu et al., 1998) and recycling of caveolae-derived vesicles back to the cell surface (Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Donnan effects generated by endocytosis promote calcium channel opening.
source: Myosin-1c may drive caveolae-derived vesicles back to the cell surface in a calcium-regulated manner because calcium channels are enriched in caveolae (Isshiki et al., 1998; Pani and Singh, 2009), the Donnan effects generated by endocytosis promote calcium channel opening (Saito et al., 2007) and calcium promotes both myosin-1c motor activity (Barylko et al., 1992; Zhu et al., 1998) and recycling of caveolae-derived vesicles back to the cell surface (Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Calcium promotes myosin-1c motor activity.
source: Myosin-1c may drive caveolae-derived vesicles back to the cell surface in a calcium-regulated manner because calcium channels are enriched in caveolae (Isshiki et al., 1998; Pani and Singh, 2009), the Donnan effects generated by endocytosis promote calcium channel opening (Saito et al., 2007) and calcium promotes both myosin-1c motor activity (Barylko et al., 1992; Zhu et al., 1998) and recycling of caveolae-derived vesicles back to the cell surface (Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Calcium promotes recycling of caveolae-derived vesicles back to the cell surface.
source: Myosin-1c may drive caveolae-derived vesicles back to the cell surface in a calcium-regulated manner because calcium channels are enriched in caveolae (Isshiki et al., 1998; Pani and Singh, 2009), the Donnan effects generated by endocytosis promote calcium channel opening (Saito et al., 2007) and calcium promotes both myosin-1c motor activity (Barylko et al., 1992; Zhu et al., 1998) and recycling of caveolae-derived vesicles back to the cell surface (Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: EGR1 can participate in a reciprocal relationship between ERK and Akt.
source: EGR1 can participate in a reciprocal relationship between ERK and Akt (Yu et al., 2011) and our findings show that cavin-3 suppresses pAkt via EGR1 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: EGR1 induces PTEN expression.
source: EGR1 induces PTEN expression (Baron et al., 2006); however, our findings show that induction of PTEN expression is not the only mechanism by which EGR1 suppresses Akt activation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Induction of PTEN expression is not the only mechanism by which EGR1 suppresses Akt activation.
source: EGR1 induces PTEN expression (Baron et al., 2006); however, our findings show that induction of PTEN expression is not the only mechanism by which EGR1 suppresses Akt activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that EGR1 suppresses pAkt in H1299 cells without restoring PTEN.

claim: EGR1 can promote ERK activation.
source: EGR1 can promote ERK activation (Shen et al., 2011) and ERK activation drives EGR1 expression (Cohen, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: ERK activation drives EGR1 expression.
source: EGR1 can promote ERK activation (Shen et al., 2011) and ERK activation drives EGR1 expression (Cohen, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The positive feedback loop between ERK and EGR1 requires cavin-3.
source: This positive feedback loop requires cavin-3 because both pERK and EGR1 expression are suppressed in the absence of cavin-3 (Figures 1–4, 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing suppression of both pERK and EGR1 upon cavin-3 loss.

claim: EGR1 down-regulates cavin-1 and caveolin-1 expression.
source: Cavin-3 and EGR1 also act within a negative feedback loop because EGR1 down-regulates cavin-1 and caveolin-1 expression (Joshi et al., 2012) and loss of either cavin-1 or caveolin-1 suppresses cavin-3 expression (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of either cavin-1 or caveolin-1 suppresses cavin-3 expression.
source: Cavin-3 and EGR1 also act within a negative feedback loop because EGR1 down-regulates cavin-1 and caveolin-1 expression (Joshi et al., 2012) and loss of either cavin-1 or caveolin-1 suppresses cavin-3 expression (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6B.

claim: Treatment with cavin-3 siRNA reduces cavin-3 protein levels by more than 80% within 3-days.
source: Treatment with cavin-3 siRNA reduces cavin-3 protein levels by more than 80% within 3-days; however, the phenotypic effects of cavin-3 depletion require 10–15 days to manifest fully (Figures 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2B.

claim: The phenotypic effects of cavin-3 depletion require 10–15 days to manifest fully.
source: Treatment with cavin-3 siRNA reduces cavin-3 protein levels by more than 80% within 3-days; however, the phenotypic effects of cavin-3 depletion require 10–15 days to manifest fully (Figures 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1-3 showing progressive changes over time.

claim: EGR1 protein levels fall slowly during the 15-day cavin-3 knockdown time course, despite rapid loss of pERK.
source: EGR1 protein levels fall slowly during the 15-day time course, despite rapid loss of pERK (Figure 2B) and the short half-life of EGR1 protein (Waters et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 2B and citation.

claim: EGR1 protein has a short half-life.
source: EGR1 protein levels fall slowly during the 15-day time course, despite rapid loss of pERK (Figure 2B) and the short half-life of EGR1 protein (Waters et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: EGR1 expression can be supported by means other than ERK.
source: EGR1 expression can be supported by means other than ERK (Hallahan et al., 1991; Guillemot et al., 2001) and these mechanisms may slow the loss of EGR1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 is not sufficient for tumorigenesis.
source: The ability of cavin-3 to influence cell signaling, proliferation, metabolism, and apoptosis provides explanations for how cavin-3 functions as a tumor suppressor; however, Cavin-3 KO animals do not show substantial increases in spontaneous cancers. These observations imply that loss of cavin-3 is not sufficient for tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Cavin-3 KO mice do not develop spontaneous cancers.

claim: Loss of cavin-3 expression is more prevalent in late-stage/high-grade cancers than in early-stage/low-grade cancers.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, loss of cavin-3 expression is more prevalent in late-stage/high-grade cancers than in early-stage/low-grade cancers (Lee et al., 2008; Caren et al., 2011; Wikman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: 35–55% of glial, lung, gastric, ovarian, breast, and colorectal cancers show hypermethylation in their cavin-3 promoters.
source: A potential clue as to the role of cavin-3 in cancer comes from the observation that 35–55% of glial, lung, gastric, ovarian, breast, and colorectal cancers show hypermethylation in their cavin-3 promoters (Xu et al., 2001; Zochbauer-Muller et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2008; Martinez et al., 2009; Tong et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Methylation of the cavin-3 promoter occurs normally in trophoblasts when they invade the endometrium during pregnancy.
source: Methylation of the cavin-3 promoter also occurs normally in trophoblasts when they invade the endometrium during pregnancy (Grigoriu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Trophoblast invasion shares many features with cancer cell metastasis.
source: Trophoblast invasion shares many features with cancer cell metastasis (Ferretti et al., 2007) and the degree of methylation in the cavin-3 promoter correlates with both trophoblast invasion potential and cancer metastasis (Wikman et al., 2012; van Dijk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The degree of methylation in the cavin-3 promoter correlates with both trophoblast invasion potential and cancer metastasis.
source: Trophoblast invasion shares many features with cancer cell metastasis (Ferretti et al., 2007) and the degree of methylation in the cavin-3 promoter correlates with both trophoblast invasion potential and cancer metastasis (Wikman et al., 2012; van Dijk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: While 41% of primary non-small cell lung carcinomas show methylation of their cavin-3 promoters, 81% of these carcinomas lack detectable cavin-3 expression by immunohistochemistry.
source: Strong selection pressure for loss of cavin-3 in cancer cells is suggested by the observation that while 41% of primary non-small cell lung carcinomas show methylation of their cavin-3 promoters, 81% of these carcinomas (N = 93) lack detectable cavin-3 expression by immunohistochemistry (Zochbauer-Muller et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Lipodystrophies have been noted in humans and animals lacking either cavin-1 or caveolin-1.
source: Lipodystrophies have also been noted in humans and animals lacking either cavin-1 or caveolin-1 (Cao et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Hayashi et al., 2009; Asterholm et al., 2012) and the association of cavin-3 with cavin-1 and caveolin-1 (Bastiani et al., 2009) combined with the dependence of cavin-3 protein on cavin-1 and caveolin-1 (Figure 6) suggests that these lipodystrophies are caused by a common mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of caveolae increases flux through the Cori cycle.
source: Loss of caveolae increases flux through the Cori cycle as evidenced by the increased rates of lactate production, hepatic gluconeogenesis and adipocyte lipolysis in Cav1−/− (Caveolin-1 KO) mice (Asterholm et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Whole body lactate production increases with age.
source: Whole body lactate production increases with age (Wallace, 2005) and loss of cavin-3 may exasperate lactate production to a point after which fatty acid demand for gluconeogenesis triggers lipolysis of triglycerides stored in adipose tissue.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Cancers that commonly elicit cachexia include lung, breast, and colorectal cancers.
source: Cancers that commonly elicit cachexia include lung, breast, and colorectal cancers (Fox et al., 2009) and these cancers frequently lack cavin-3 expression (Xu et al., 2001; Zochbauer-Muller et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lung, breast, and colorectal cancers frequently lack cavin-3 expression.
source: Cancers that commonly elicit cachexia include lung, breast, and colorectal cancers (Fox et al., 2009) and these cancers frequently lack cavin-3 expression (Xu et al., 2001; Zochbauer-Muller et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The absence of cavin-3 in tumors may predispose patients to the development of cancer-associated cachexia.
source: Thus, the absence of cavin-3 in tumors may predispose patients to the development of cancer-associated cachexia, a condition that is the immediate cause of death for more than 20% of all cancer patients (Tisdale, 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the correlation between cavin-3 loss and cachexia.

source: Recent work has shown that caveolae of different tissues and cell types have different cavin compositions (Bastiani et al., 2009; Hansen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The fibroblasts and epithelial cells examined in this study express cavin-1 and cavin-3, but lack cavin-2 and cavin-4.
source: The fibroblasts and epithelial cells examined here express cavin-1 and cavin-3, but lack cavin-2 and cavin-4.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations in the study.

claim: Adipocytes abundantly express cavin-2.
source: By contrast, adipocytes abundantly express cavin-2, myocytes have abundant cavin-4 and endothelial cells have different compositions depending upon tissue localization (Stan et al., 1999; Ogata et al., 2008; Bastiani et al., 2009; Hansen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Use of different cavins may provide alternative linkages that can support surface caveolae or provide novel functions for caveolae in different cell types.
source: Use of different cavins may provide alternative linkages that can support surface caveolae or provide novel functions for caveolae in different cell types.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed diversity in cavin composition.

claim: Cavin-3 plays a critical role in the signal transduction function of caveolae.
source: We show here that cavin-3 plays a critical role in the signal transduction function of caveolae and that cells, which normally express cavin-3, rely upon cavin-3 for normal ERK and Akt signaling with consequences for cell metabolism, apoptosis, and cell proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented in the study.
